 I'm Charis from the CX Solution & Product Learning team, and I am excited to announce the launch of our latest course, Positioning Autonomous Unified Commerce , now available on learning.sap.com ! 
 🌟 About This Course 
 The commerce landscape is changing fast. Agentic AI is reshaping buyer demand, and execution — not just discovery or conversion — has become the new competitive frontier. This course introduces SAP Autonomous Unified Commerce: SAP's vision for moving beyond connected systems toward a fully autonomous execution engine that makes real-time decisions across pricing, inventory, and fulfillment, while continuously learning from outcomes. 
 In just 22 minutes, you will gain the language and understanding needed to position this solution confidently — whether you are speaking with customers, partners, or internal stakeholders. 
 📝 Course Details

 Duration 22 min 
 Units 1 
 Achievement Leads to Achievement 
 Access Free on learning.sap.com

 By the end of this course, you will be able to: 
 Identify the key challenges facing modern commerce teams in the age of agentic AI, and explain why execution has become the critical competitive differentiator 
 Explain how SAP Autonomous Unified Commerce addresses those challenges through connected AI agents built on a shared foundation of customer, product, and operational data 
 Describe how Experience Agents, Execution Agents, and Optimization Agents work together to drive trust, loyalty, and profitability across the full commerce lifecycle

You will explore how Experience Agents, Execution Agents, and Optimization Agents work together across the commerce lifecycle, and how Joule-powered assistants bring autonomous decisions to the surface for commerce teams.

It is equally valuable for commerce practitioners and digital commerce managers who want to understand how SAP's AI agent framework supports autonomous, end-to-end commerce execution. No prior technical knowledge is required.

title: Relembre a palestra: Além do Go-Live, a camada da adoção digital #SITCWB2026
author: AdrianoCWB
text:
No dia 7 de novembro, no Auditório Gregor Mendel da PUCPR, Rodrigo Cordeiro, Head de Transformação de Negócios na Numen, apresentou no SAP Inside Track Curitiba 2026 a palestra "Além do Go-Live: Maximizando a Adoção Digital e o ROI com WalkMe". 
 Sobre a palestra 
 Toda transformação SAP tem duas histórias: a do projeto (escopo, orçamento, go-live no prazo) e a do uso real (seis meses depois, parte da equipe ainda usa planilha paralela). Rodrigo mostrou que o gap entre as duas é a distância entre o sistema estar certo e a pessoa saber o que fazer com ele no momento exato. 
 Segundo dados do WalkMe citados na palestra, US$ 104 milhões foram desperdiçados em 2024 com tecnologia subutilizada, cada colaborador perde 51 dias por ano com fricção digital e 70% das iniciativas de transformação não geram o valor planejado. 
 SAP BTM e a camada de adoção 
 O SAP BTM integra três camadas: processos (SAP Signavio), arquitetura (SAP LeanIX) e adoção (WalkMe), que foi o foco da palestra. O WalkMe é uma plataforma de adoção digital que fica sobre a aplicação, sem alterar o código, para identificar onde a pessoa trava e guiá-la na hora. Foi adquirido pela SAP em setembro de 2024 e se apoia em três pilares: dados, ação e experiência. 
 WalkMe e Joule: rivais ou parceiros? 
 A resposta foi que não é um ou outro. A Joule responde "o que eu preciso fazer?" a partir de uma pergunta do usuário. O WalkMe responde "como faço isso nesta tela?", de forma proativa e contextual. Na ideia da palestra, a Joule é o cérebro e o WalkMe é a camada de experiência. 
 Três lentes e o Learning Arc 
 Consultor: garantir que o usuário saiba operar no dia 1 é entrega, escopo e diferencial. 
 Usuário: a ajuda aparece quando ele trava, e não em um treinamento genérico feito meses antes. 
 Líder: a métrica de sucesso deixa de ser "foi ao ar" e passa a ser "está sendo usado direito". 
 Learning Arc: treinamento dentro da aplicação, com simulações em modo Demo, Practice e Test, e medição de conclusão e de quedas em quiz. 
 Para levar 
 Go-live não é a linha de chegada, é o começo do uso real. 
 Adoção digital é uma entrega do projeto, não um detalhe. 
 Meça o uso, não a presença no treinamento. 
 Sobre o palestrante 
 Rodrigo Cordeiro, Head de Transformação de Negócios na Numen e professor de pós-graduação em arquitetura funcional, com nove certificações SAP. 
 Assista à palestra no YouTube (de 1:20 a 40:19 do vídeo): https://youtu.be/6kfJHxQN140?t=80 
 Veja todas as palestras no post índice: https://community.sap.com/t5/curitiba-blog-posts/sap-inside-track-curitiba-2026-relembre-as-palestras-sitcwb/ba-p/14522453 
 #SITCWB2026 #SAPCommunity #SAPCommunityCWB #SAPBTM #WalkMe

title: SAP Business Data Cloud: Transforming Enterprise Data into Intelligent Business Decisions
author: sraji2486
text:
Introduction 
 Organizations today use different applications to manage their business operations. Finance, procurement, sales, human resources, and other departments generate large amounts of data every day. Although this information is valuable, it is often stored across different systems, making it difficult to get a complete view of business performance. 
 For example, an organization may use SAP S/4HANA for finance and procurement, SAP SuccessFactors for employee information, and SAP Analytics Cloud (SAC) for reporting. When management needs a consolidated report, data from these systems must be connected, prepared, and presented in a meaningful way. 
 This is where SAP Business Data Cloud (SAP BDC) comes into the picture. 
 SAP Business Data Cloud is a cloud-based solution that brings together SAP and non-SAP data, analytics, planning, and AI capabilities. It helps organizations make better use of their existing data while maintaining its business meaning. 
 In this blog, let's explore SAP Business Data Cloud, its key components, how it works, and how it can be used in practical business scenarios. 
 What is SAP Business Data Cloud? 
 SAP Business Data Cloud is a fully managed cloud solution designed to connect and manage business data from different sources. 
 It brings together existing SAP technologies such as SAP Datasphere, SAP Analytics Cloud, and SAP Business Warehouse, along with SAP Databricks and other capabilities. 
 The main idea behind SAP BDC is to make business data available for different purposes without repeatedly creating the same data models and business logic. 
 For example, finance teams can use financial data for reporting, while procurement teams can use purchasing information to analyze supplier performance. Both teams can work with trusted business data while meeting their individual requirements. 
 One important point is that SAP Business Data Cloud is not simply another reporting tool or a replacement for SAP Datasphere. It provides a broader environment that connects data management, analytics, planning, and AI. 
 Key Components of SAP Business Data Cloud 
 SAP Business Data Cloud brings together different technologies, with each component supporting a specific business requirement. 
 SAP Datasphere 
 SAP Datasphere helps organizations connect data from different systems, create data models, and maintain business context. It allows developers to prepare and share data for analytical requirements. 
 SAP Analytics Cloud 
 SAP Analytics Cloud supports dashboards, reporting, data visualization, and enterprise planning. Business users can use it to analyze performance and monitor important KPIs. 
 SAP Business Warehouse 
 SAP BW supports existing enterprise data warehouse requirements. Organizations can continue using their existing BW investments while exploring modernization options through SAP BDC. 
 SAP Databricks 
 SAP Databricks provides capabilities for data engineering, machine learning, data science, and AI. It helps organizations perform advanced analysis using SAP and non-SAP data. 
 SAP HANA Cloud 
 SAP HANA Cloud provides database and data processing capabilities. It also supports application development and advanced analytical requirements. 
 SAP Master Data Governance 
 SAP Master Data Governance helps organizations maintain consistent and reliable master data across business applications. 
 These components work together to provide a connected data and analytics environment. Organizations can select the capabilities based on their requirements and existing technology landscape. 
 Understanding Data Products 
 One of the important concepts in SAP Business Data Cloud is data products. 
 In simple terms, a data product is a prepared collection of business data that can be reused by different teams and applications. 
 In traditional data environments, developers often extract individual tables and create separate models for every reporting requirement. This can result in repeated development work and inconsistent calculations. 
 Data products help reduce this effort by providing structured information with business meaning, metadata, and documentation. 
 For example, consider a finance data product containing general ledger information, company codes, financial documents, and cost centre details. 
 Instead of preparing the same information separately for multiple reports, different teams can use the available data product for their requirements. 
 SAP also provides ready-to-use data products from supported SAP applications, which can help organizations reduce the time required to prepare data. 
 The main benefits are reusability, consistency, better data management, and easier access to trusted business information. 
 Practical Example: Building an Enterprise Analytics Solution 
 Let's consider a company that wants to create a consolidated management dashboard using finance, procurement, and HR information. 
 The company currently uses: 

 SAP S/4HANA for finance and procurement. 

 SAP SuccessFactors for HR. 

 SAP Datasphere for data integration and modelling. 

 SAP Analytics Cloud for dashboards and reporting. 
 The requirement is to bring the required information together and provide management with a single view of business performance. 
 The implementation can be approached in the following way. 
 Step 1: Identify the source systems 
 First, identify the systems and data required for reporting. 
 For example, finance information may include actual expenses, GL balances, and cost centres. Procurement may require purchase orders, supplier details, and invoice information. HR may require employee details and department information. 
 Understanding the source systems and business requirements is important before starting the integration. 
 Step 2: Integrate the required data 
 The next step is to make the required information available through SAP BDC. 
 Depending on the source system and requirement, organizations can use available SAP data products, data federation, replication, and supported integration methods. 
 For example, finance and procurement information can be obtained from SAP S/4HANA, while employee information can be obtained from SAP SuccessFactors. 
 The integration approach should be selected based on data volume, refresh frequency, and business requirements. 
 Step 3: Create data models using SAP Datasphere 
 Once the data is available, SAP Datasphere can be used to prepare the required business models. 
 For example, finance information can be connected with cost centre and company code details to calculate department-wise expenditure. 
 Similarly, procurement information can be organized to analyze supplier performance and purchasing activities. 
 These models help maintain common business definitions and make information available for different reporting requirements. 
 Step 4: Develop dashboards using SAP Analytics Cloud 
 After preparing the data models, SAP Analytics Cloud can be used to develop dashboards. 
 A management dashboard may include: 

 Total revenue and expenses. 

 Actual versus budget. 

 Department-wise expenditure. 

 Purchase order details. 

 Supplier performance. 

 Employee headcount. 
 Management can use these dashboards to understand business performance without checking multiple applications separately. 
 For example, finance managers can compare actual expenses against budget, while procurement managers can review purchasing trends. 
 Step 5: Explore AI and advanced analytics 
 Once the organization has a reliable data foundation, it can explore machine learning and AI capabilities. 
 For example, historical procurement information can be analyzed to identify unusual purchasing patterns or predict future requirements. 
 SAP Databricks can support data engineering and machine learning activities, while SAP's AI capabilities can help users work with business information more effectively. 
 This example shows how different SAP technologies can work together to support an end-to-end analytics requirement. 
 Zero-Copy Data Sharing 
 Another important capability of SAP Business Data Cloud is zero-copy data sharing. 
 In traditional data environments, information is often copied from one platform to another before it can be used for reporting or advanced analysis. This can increase storage requirements and create additional data maintenance activities. 
 SAP Business Data Cloud Connect supports sharing data and metadata between SAP BDC and supported external platforms without creating additional physical copies for supported scenarios. 
 For example, an organization using SAP Databricks for machine learning can access shared SAP business data for advanced analysis. 
 This helps reduce unnecessary data movement and allows organizations to make better use of their existing data platforms. 
 However, zero-copy does not mean that every integration is completely free from data movement. The actual approach depends on the supported platform and integration requirements. 
 SAP BW Modernization 
 Many organizations have been using SAP Business Warehouse for several years. These environments contain important business data, reports, queries, and transformation logic. 
 Replacing the entire BW environment can be expensive and time-consuming. 
 SAP Business Data Cloud provides modernization options that allow organizations to continue using existing BW investments while gradually adopting cloud-based capabilities. 
 For example, an organization using SAP BW for financial reporting can review its existing data models and identify which data assets can be reused through supported SAP BDC integration capabilities. 
 This allows organizations to modernize their data environment step by step instead of replacing everything immediately. 
 The main objective is to protect existing investments while taking advantage of newer data and analytics capabilities. 
 Industry Applications 
 SAP Business Data Cloud can support different industries because most organizations depend on information from multiple business systems. 
 Some practical examples include: 
 Manufacturing: Combining production, inventory, procurement, and financial information to improve operational visibility. 
 Banking: Connecting customer, transaction, and financial information to support risk analysis. 
 Retail: Combining sales, inventory, and customer information to understand demand and improve planning. 
 Healthcare: Connecting financial and operational information to improve resource management. 
 Oil and Gas: Combining maintenance, procurement, workforce, and financial information to understand operational costs. 
 For example, an oil and gas company may want to analyze maintenance expenditure across different operational locations. By combining maintenance, procurement, and finance information, management can compare costs and identify areas that require further investigation. 
 These use cases show how connected business data can support better decisions across different departments. 
 Challenges and Best Practices 
 Although SAP Business Data Cloud provides several capabilities, organizations should consider a few important points before implementation. 
 Data quality: Incorrect or incomplete source data can affect reporting results. Source data should be validated before creating analytical models. 
 Security: Finance, HR, and operational information may have different access requirements. Appropriate roles and authorizations should be maintained. 
 Integration: The integration approach should be selected based on the source system, data volume, and required refresh frequency. 
 Performance: Data models, joins, and refresh schedules should be reviewed to maintain good reporting performance. 
 Skills and knowledge: Implementation teams should understand the relevant SAP technologies, including Datasphere, Analytics Cloud, data integration, and security. 
 It is also better to start with a small business use case, such as finance

title: Material Ledger Activity Update 2 → 1 (CON2): Benefit vs. Loss of Multilevel Actual Activity Prices
author: Jiecang2024
text:
Dear SAP experts, 
 Our users want to see actual activity prices at production order level for cost analysis. We understand that this requires changing the Material Ledger "Activity Update" setting from 2 to 1 and using CON2. The same note states that after the switch, actual activity prices are no longer reflected in the multilevel (material) view and appear only at production order level.( https://me.sap.com/notes/2240562/E ) 

 We would like to understand whether this trade-off is worthwhile before deciding on a switch in production. 
 Planned test approach: Copy production data to a test system after a period has been closed and settled. 
 Switch from 2 to 1 and activate CON2 at the period boundary (previous period closed, new period without postings). 
 Post a few new production orders in the new period, and run price determination, CON2 and settlement. 
 Compare CKM3, cost component split and order variances before and after the switch. 
 We are aware that switching within an open period is not supported, so we only intend to test at a period boundary. 
 Questions 
 1. Benefit: After the switch, what exactly is available at order level that is not available with setting 2 (for example, actual activity prices and activity price differences by order)? Are there any standard reports for this analysis (for example, CKM3 or the cost component split)? 
 2. Loss at material level: Which information is no longer available in the multilevel view after the switch? Does this affect material price determination, inventory valuation, or the actual cost component split of finished and semi-finished goods? 
 Risks: What are the known risks and side effects of the switch, especially for in-process orders, orders spanning the switch period, and TECO orders with errors in COFC or historical goods movement errors (for example, CO688)? 
 3. Prerequisites: Is it mandatory that no open production orders exist at the time of the switch? If some orders cannot be closed, what is the impact? 
 4. Reversibility: Can the setting be switched back from 1 to 2 later? If yes, under which conditions? 
 5.Recommendation: Does SAP recommend this switch only to meet the requirement of order-level actual activity prices? Is there an alternative that provides order-level analysis without losing the multilevel view? 
 6. Testing: Is our test approach (copy after period close, switch at the period boundary) sufficient, or is there an SAP-recommended procedure or checklist for validating the switch? 
 Thank you in advance for your guidance. 
 Best regards

title: SAP and planqc Bring Quantum Computing into Business Processes
author: SAP News
text:
MUNICH — SAP SE (NYSE: SAP) is stepping up its quantum computing activities and expanding its collaboration with Munich-based quantum computer manufacturer planqc. 
 Innovation at SAP helps organizations turn technology into an engine for business innovation 

 Learn more 

 At Quantum Day Munich, which is being run by SAP, the two companies are demonstrating for the first time how a planqc neutral-atom quantum computer can be integrated into an SAP software environment. SAP is also showcasing its first quantum agents and establishing a dedicated quantum team in Munich. Starting in 2027, the companies plan to test initial business scenarios on actual planqc quantum hardware. 

 SAP sees the potential for quantum computing to reach performance levels relevant to SAP software applications before the end of this decade. The company is, therefore, exploring how quantum computing can complement classical optimization, simulation and AI. Munich offers a dense ecosystem of leading research institutions, specialized suppliers, startups and industry partners. 

 “Quantum computing opens up new ways to solve complex problems. We see neutral-atom quantum computers in particular as a promising approach to scalable quantum computing,” said Dr. Carsten Polenz, Global Head of Quantum, SAP. “What matters now is embedding this computing power into business processes and making it accessible to customers. With planqc, we can develop directly on real quantum hardware and shorten the path to real-world business applications.” 

 The technical foundation is a cloud interface connecting the SAP software landscape with planqc’s quantum computing environment. The hybrid architecture combines classical solvers, quantum simulators and real quantum hardware. At today’s Quantum Day Munich, SAP and planqc are demonstrating for the first time how this works successfully in a real-world application scenario. In optimizing the loading of a delivery vehicle, an optimization task is transferred from an SAP software logistics process to the planqc environment and computed on a quantum simulator. The resulting loading plan is then fed back into the SAP software process. In the future, such scenarios are expected to run directly on a neutral-atom quantum computer. 

 On the same technological foundation, SAP is developing its first quantum agents. They are designed to capture business objectives and constraints and orchestrate appropriate solution methods. Users should, therefore, be able to address business problems without having to program quantum hardware themselves or develop specialized quantum expertise. The focus is on the business decision, not the underlying computing technology. 

 “Europe has a strong research base and essential parts of the technology supply chain for quantum computers,” said Dr. Alexander Glätzle, co-founder and CEO of planqc. “The challenge now is to turn these strengths into competitive products and real-world applications. With SAP, we are bringing our neutral-atom quantum computers to where companies manage complex business processes. This allows companies to build expertise and develop real-world use cases while the technology matures, rather than waiting until powerful quantum computers become available.”
